planting.note: Set out rooted stem or rhizome cuttings in spring into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; like French tarragon, this tetraploid selection almost never sets viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or rhizome divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, since this tetraploid tarragon selection almost never flowers normally and never produces viable seed. Epicure is a smooth-leaved, strongly aromatic tarragon clone whose essential oil is dominated by methyl chavicol, giving it a cleaner, more concentrated anise-licorice flavor than many run-of-the-mill nursery tarragon starts sold simply as 'French tarragon.' Harvest by snipping young stem tips through the growing season and expect the top growth to die back completely over winter, re-emerging from the crown once soil warms in spring. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and multiply stock, since seed propagation is not an option.
sources: Frontiers in Pharmacology — Artemisia dracunculus: A Review of Its Traditional Uses, Phytochemistry and Pharmacology

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively to keep the true lemon scent, since seed-grown plants can revert toward plain winter savory.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since seed-raised plants of this form can lose the true lemon character. Lemon Winter Savory forms the same tidy, semi-evergreen mound of narrow dark leaves as standard winter savory, but crushed foliage releases a clean, sweet citrus fragrance in place of the usual resinous, peppery savory smell, making it a workable substitute for lemon thyme in the kitchen. Because the lemon flavor fades under long cooking, add sprigs near the end of cooking for fish, poultry, or bean dishes rather than simmering them in from the start. Clip the plant back after its small summer flowers fade to keep the mound tight and encourage fresh, strongly scented new growth for the following season.

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly after the last frost once soil has warmed; Saturn is a field cultivar bred in Poland for essential-oil production and performs like ordinary summer savory in the home garden.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed, thinning seedlings to stand 8 to 12 inches apart. Saturn is a Polish-bred field cultivar of summer savory developed for industrial essential-oil extraction, and its foliage carries an unusually high concentration of carvacrol and gamma-terpinene, giving a sharper, more concentrated peppery-herbal bite than an average garden-strain summer savory. In the kitchen it is used exactly like common summer savory in bean, lentil, and sausage dishes, but because of its stronger oil content it can be used a bit more sparingly. For the most concentrated flavor and oil content, cut whole plants for drying right at the start of flowering.
sources: Institute of Natural Fibres and Medicinal Plants, Poznan

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; this compact cultivar is well suited to containers and small garden edges where standard summer savory would sprawl too wide.

directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for an extra-early container crop. Midget is a compact, densely branched selection of summer savory that stays only about 10 to 12 inches tall with proportionally more leaf mass per plant than standard seed strains, making it well suited to pots, window boxes, and tight raised-bed edges. Its narrow, dark green leaves carry the same peppery, thyme-and-mint-tinged summer savory flavor as the full-sized species and can be harvested continuously through the season. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep the dense habit tidy and to delay flowering, which lets flavor hold longer than it does on unpinched plants.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively to keep the true violet-blue flower color.

directions: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, cutting the woody stems back hard in early spring to keep growth dense. Blue Winter Savory is a selection of common winter savory grown as much for its show of pale violet-blue flower spikes in summer as for the kitchen, with the same narrow, hairy-edged, strongly aromatic green leaves and upright bushy habit as the species. The leaves carry the familiar robust, resinous, peppery winter savory flavor and can be used interchangeably with the plain species in bean and slow-cooked meat dishes. Protect the crown from standing winter moisture, since like other winter savory selections it is far more tolerant of cold and drought than of wet feet.
